newsitem.title: FRANCE: France said considering voting system reform.
newsitem.headline: France said considering voting system reform.

text.p: France is considering changing its parliamentary election system to add an element of proportional representation that could give seats to the Greens and the far-right National Front, a newspaper said on Friday.

The daily Le Monde quoted conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe as telling parliamentary floor leaders on Thursday that he had for some time been weighing the reform -- a change also advocated by the opposition Socialists and Communists.

The most fervent supporters of reform are smaller parties such as the anti-immigrant National Front and the divided ecologist movement, which have been kept out of parliament by the current twin-ballot single-member constituency system, which favours larger groups.

Bruno Megret, a senior National Front leader, welcomed in a statement the report of a possible electoral reform but said it showed how frightened the centre-right government was of his party's rise in public support.
Under the current system, a candidate must win more than half the votes in the first round to be elected outright to the National Assembly. The two top candidates go on to a run-off.
The National Front failed to win a single seat in the last general election in 1993 despite polling 12.5 percent of the popular vote.
Le Monde said the Interior Ministry was already studying a reform. There was no immediate official comment.

But National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin backed a reform on Friday, telling a ruling Gaullist party meeting: "We will at some point have to find a way of ensuring that all major political currents are represented in parliament."

French political parties have fought over the voting system since the late president Charles de Gaulle abolished proportional representation in 1958 to restore political stability after an era of revolving-door cabinets dependent on shifting alliances among a large number of parties.

The late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand restored proportional representation for the 1986 general election, but the conservative government of then prime minister Jacques Chirac reverted to the constituency system the following year.

Le Monde said Juppe gave no details of the proposed reform. Floor leaders said it could entail electing deputies in the most populated regions by proportional representation while keeping single-member constituencies in rural areas.

Another idea could be adding to the National Assembly's 577 seats a number of members elected by proportional representation -- with the drawback of entailing unpopular extra costs at a time of budget austerity.
